title: Pre-Qualification vs Pre-Approval: Choosing a Mortgage Lender
description: Pre-qualification vs pre-approval, how to compare Loan Estimates from multiple lenders, and how agent lender referrals work when you pick a lender.
body:
Before you get serious about touring homes, it helps to talk with a mortgage lender. The terms get mixed up, though, and choosing a lender can feel like a guess.

This post covers the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval, why it pays to compare Loan Estimates from more than one lender, and how a lender referral from an agent fits in. I'm not a lender, and none of this is lending advice. It's an explanation of how the process works.

## Pre-qualification vs pre-approval

{{img:0}}

These two words get used as if they mean the same thing. They don't.

A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow, based on information you tell a lender. Nothing is verified at that stage.

A pre-approval goes further. The lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter. That review is the real difference between the two.

One caution: a pre-approval letter is not a final loan commitment. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting, and your finances staying the same until closing. That is why lenders and agents often tell buyers to avoid opening new credit, financing furniture, or changing jobs from the time you apply through closing.

If you want to see how a rate and a price might turn into a monthly payment while you gather documents, the [mortgage calculator](/mortgage-calculator) on this site lets you try your own numbers.

## Why you should compare Loan Estimates from multiple lenders

After you apply, a lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days. It is a standard three-page form, so estimates from different lenders can be compared side by side.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau encourages borrowers to get Loan Estimates from more than one lender and compare them, because interest rates and fees can differ from lender to lender. Their [Owning a Home guides](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) walk through how to read the form.

For context, the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate was 7.28% for the week of 2026-10-01, according to Freddie Mac via the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED). That is a national average. The rate and fees you are offered depend on your own details, and two lenders can quote you different numbers for the same loan.

When you line up estimates, look at:

- The interest rate and the loan type
- The lender's fees and other closing costs
- The estimated monthly payment
- The cash you would need at closing

Closing costs typically run 2 to 4 percent of the purchase price, plus earnest money and moving costs. Fees are worth comparing for that reason.

You may worry that several applications will hurt your credit. Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Comparing lenders close together is usually less harmful than spreading applications out over months. Ask each lender how this works for your situation.

The comparison continues after you pick a lender. At least 3 business days before closing, the lender must send you the Closing Disclosure. Compare it with your Loan Estimate and ask questions about anything that changed.

## Types of lenders and loan programs

{{img:1}}

Mortgage lenders include banks, credit unions, mortgage brokers and online lenders. A mortgage broker compares offers from several lenders on your behalf. Each type works a little differently, so it is fair to ask any of them how they get paid and what they would charge you.

A few program facts are worth knowing as you ask questions:

- Private mortgage insurance is typically required on conventional loans when the down payment is under 20 percent.
- FHA loans allow a down payment as low as 3.5 percent.
- VA loans typically require no down payment and no monthly mortgage insurance, though a funding fee may apply. The [VA home loans](https://www.va.gov/housing-assistance/home-loans/) page explains eligibility.
- The [Tennessee Housing Development Agency](https://www.thda.org) offers home loan programs through participating lenders, so ask any lender you are considering whether they take part.

Whether any of these programs applies to you is a question for a licensed lender and the official program sources.

## Asking an agent for lender referrals

It is normal to ask your real estate agent for lender names. Your agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work.

The choice is yours, though. You are free to use any lender you like. A referral is a starting point, not a requirement, and I would not treat it as an endorsement. I would still get a Loan Estimate from at least one lender you find on your own, and compare.

Some questions to ask any lender, whether you found them yourself or through a referral:

- Will you give me a pre-approval based on a review of my documents, or only a pre-qualification?
- How quickly will I get a Loan Estimate after I apply?
- Do you take part in state programs such as THDA's?
- How will you communicate with me and with my agent during the process?

Also, wire fraud is real. When it is time to send closing funds, verify wire instructions by phone using a number you already trust, and never rely on emailed wire instructions.

If you want to check that a real estate professional is licensed, the [Tennessee Real Estate Commission](https://www.tn.gov/commerce/regboards/trec.html) is the official source.

## Your next step

Start with a pre-approval conversation, collect Loan Estimates from a few lenders, and compare them line by line. For local numbers to read alongside those conversations, the [market data page](/market-data) covers the I-65 corridor.

If you would like help thinking through the process, fill out the form on [Get matched with homes](/buy#form). I will schedule a call, and you will be talking with me within the next 48 hours. You can also [contact me](/contact) directly with questions.

Scott Davis, REALTOR® with Hive Nashville

faq.q: What is the difference between pre-qualification and pre-approval?
faq.a: A pre-qualification is a quick estimate of what you might be able to borrow, based on information you tell a lender. A pre-approval goes further: the lender reviews your documents and credit before issuing a letter.

faq.q: Is a pre-approval letter a guarantee of a loan?
faq.a: No. A pre-approval letter is not a final loan commitment. Final approval depends on the appraisal, underwriting, and your finances staying the same until closing.

faq.q: Does comparing mortgage lenders hurt my credit?
faq.a: Credit-scoring models generally treat several mortgage inquiries made within a short period as a single inquiry. Comparing lenders close together is usually less harmful than spreading applications out. Ask each lender how this works for your situation.

faq.q: Do I have to use the lender my agent recommends?
faq.a: No. Your agent can share names of lenders they have seen do good work, but you choose your own lender and are free to use any lender you like.

faq.q: How soon will I get a Loan Estimate after I apply?
faq.a: A lender must give you a Loan Estimate within three business days after you apply. It is a standard three-page form, so you can compare estimates from different lenders side by side.
